Master Charles Bates, horrified by the crime of Sikes, began to ponder whether an honest existence might not, after all, be the better one. Having decided that it assuredly was, he abandoned the haunts of his former life, determined to redeem the past in a fresh field of endeavour. For a while he laboured mightily and endured much hardship; but a cheerful temper and an upright aim brought him success at last. From a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he has risen to be the jolliest young grazier in the whole of Northamptonshire.

And now the hand setting down these words grows hesitant as its labour nears an end, and would prolong a little further the weaving of these adventures.

Gladly would I remain a while with some of those whose company I have kept so long, and partake of their happiness by attempting to portray it. I would reveal Rose Maylie in the grace and blossom of her early womanhood, casting upon her quiet course through life a gentle radiance that touched all who walked beside her and entered their hearts. I would depict her as the delight and spirit of the fireside gathering and the merry summer party. I would accompany her across the hot fields at midday and hear her sweet voice speaking softly during an evening stroll beneath the moon. I would observe her goodness and benevolence away from home, and her smiling, tireless performance of household duties within it. I would picture her and her dead sister’s child, content in their mutual affection, spending hours together recalling the friends so sorrowfully lost. Once more I would call up the happy little faces gathered at her knee and listen to their cheerful chatter. I would remember the sound of that clear laughter and summon the sympathetic tear shining in her gentle blue eye. All these, and a thousand expressions and smiles, and movements of speech and thought—I would gladly bring back every one.

How Mr. Brownlow continued, day after day, to enrich his adopted child’s mind with knowledge, loving him ever more deeply as his character unfolded and the seeds of everything he desired for him flourished; how he discovered fresh likenesses to his early friend, stirring old memories in his heart, sorrowful yet sweet and consoling; how the two orphans, schooled by suffering, kept its lessons alive in kindness towards others, affection for each other, and earnest gratitude to Him who had guarded and sustained them—all these are things that have no need of telling.

He sprang to his feet and caught her arm roughly. “Show me the man. Which one is he? Point to him. I have to see him!” he cried. Just then, however, the Duke of Berwick’s four-in-hand passed between them, and by the time the view was clear again, the carriage had rolled out of the park.

“He has gone,” Sibyl murmured sorrowfully. “I wish you could have seen him.”

“So do I; for as surely as there is a God above, if he ever harms you, I will kill him.”

She stared at him, horrified. He said the words again. They sliced the air like a knife. People nearby began to stare, and a lady beside her gave a little titter.

“Come away, Jim, please come away,” she whispered. As she moved through the crowd, he followed stubbornly. He was pleased with what he had said.

On reaching the Achilles Statue, she faced him. Pity in her eyes turned to laughter upon her lips, and she shook her head. “You are silly, Jim, perfectly silly—nothing but an ill-tempered boy. How can you utter such dreadful things? You have no idea what you are saying. You are merely jealous and cruel. Oh, I wish you would fall in love yourself! Love makes us good, and those words were wicked.”

“I am sixteen,” he replied, “and I know what I’m doing. Mother is no use to you. She doesn’t know how to protect you. Now I wish I weren’t going to Australia at all. I’ve half a mind to throw the whole business over. I would, if my articles weren’t already signed.”

“Oh, don’t be so solemn, Jim. You sound like a hero in those absurd melodramas Mother loved acting in. I won’t fight with you. I’ve seen him, and oh, seeing him is complete happiness! We mustn’t quarrel. I know you could never hurt someone I love, could you?”

“Not while you love him, I suppose,” he replied sulkily.

“I shall love him always!” she exclaimed.

“And what of him?”

“Always too!”

“He’d better.”

She recoiled from him. Then she laughed, laying her hand upon his arm. After all, he was only a boy.

At Marble Arch they called an omnibus, which set them down near their shabby house in Euston Road. It was past five, and Sibyl needed to rest for two hours before her performance. Jim insisted on it. He said he preferred to say goodbye without their mother there. She was certain to make a scene, and he loathed scenes of any description.

“April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction, and though I had fully foreseen it, it gave me the most unqualified pleasure. On its previous course it had reached approximately the twentieth parallel of south latitude, when it suddenly veered eastward at an acute angle. It maintained this direction all day, remaining almost, if not precisely, within the plane of the moon’s ellipse. One circumstance deserving notice was the very distinct swaying of the car produced by this alteration of course—a motion that persisted, with varying force, for many hours.

“April 13th. Once more greatly frightened by the recurrence of the loud crackling sound that alarmed me on the tenth. Considered the matter at length, without reaching any satisfactory explanation. The apparent diameter of the earth has diminished greatly, now subtending an angle barely exceeding twenty-five degrees as seen from the balloon. The moon remained wholly invisible, being almost at my zenith. I continued within the plane of the ellipse, though with scarcely any eastward advance.

“April 14th. The earth’s diameter is shrinking with extraordinary speed. To-day I became firmly persuaded that the balloon was actually ascending the line of apsides towards perigee; that is, following a direct route to the moon at the point in its orbit nearest the earth. The moon itself lay immediately overhead and was therefore concealed from sight. Condensing the atmosphere required immense and prolonged exertion.

“April 15th. Even the shapes of oceans and continents upon the earth could no longer be distinguished with anything resembling clearness. At about noon I heard, for the third time, the terrifying noise that had previously so bewildered me. This time it lasted several moments, increasing in force as it went on. At last, as I stood stunned and terrified, awaiting some hideous destruction whose nature I could not guess, the car shook with extreme violence. An enormous burning mass of an unidentified substance rushed roaring and booming past the balloon with the sound of a thousand thunderclaps. Once my terror and amazement had somewhat abated, I readily supposed it to be a vast volcanic fragment hurled from the world I was rapidly nearing. Most probably it belonged to that peculiar class of objects sometimes found upon the earth and called meteoric stones for lack of a fitter name.

“April 16th. To-day, peering upward as well as I was able through the side windows in turn, I saw with immense delight a tiny part of the moon’s disk projecting, as it seemed, on every side beyond the balloon’s immense circumference.
